1268.title: George MacDonald
1268.hook: a Scottish storyteller of God's relentless, fatherly love
1268.howItsDone: Christians who read George MacDonald often read his fairy tales and his Unspoken Sermons side by side, and some families read his children's books aloud together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chesterton's fairyland: the plain world, as strange and chosen as any story. Your line was the world is strange.

A young princess climbs a stair in her own castle she's never noticed before, and at the top finds an old, beautiful woman, spinning. The woman says she's the princess's great-great-grandmother. Her nurse doesn't believe a word of it. Later, the grandmother gives the girl a thread so fine she can hardly see it, and tells her to follow it whenever she's afraid. Deep in the dark, under the mountain, the thread leads exactly where she needs to go. That's The Princess and the Goblin, by George MacDonald, a Scottish minister who became a storyteller.

For MacDonald, God's love was like that thread: hard to see, and impossible to break. He called God Father, and meant it at full strength. A good father doesn't stop loving a child who runs off. He keeps going after them. MacDonald heard that in Jesus's story of the son who wastes everything and turns for home, where the father sees him "when he was yet a great way off," and runs. In his Unspoken Sermons, MacDonald takes on a line from Hebrews that can sound frightening: "For our God is a consuming fire." Some readers hear a threat. MacDonald heard love. The fire, he said, burns against everything in us that isn't love, our selfishness, our lies, our hardness, and it won't stop burning until those are gone. But it never burns against us. It's the fire of a love that refuses to give up on what it loves: relentless, which here means tireless, not harsh. Some Christians found MacDonald too hopeful. He was willing to hope that this love might reach everyone in the end, and others pushed back on that, and still do. His admirers say he made God's fatherhood feel like coming home. Either way, he told it through fairy tales: goblins and mountains, a North Wind, a princess with a thread. He seems to have trusted that a child, or a grown-up who'd forgotten how to be one, might understand love through a story before following an argument.

Who came, and what did it feel like back then to hear that part? Sit with that scene for a while, and if you pray, give thanks for whoever first read to you.

Your line: love will not let go. Like a thread too fine to see, and too strong to break. Go gently.

1269.title: Barth's simple summary
1269.hook: Karl Barth, asked to sum up his vast theology, is remembered for naming a children's song, Jesus loves me
1269.howItsDone: "Jesus Loves Me" is sung in Sunday schools and children's services across different churches, and some adults sing or say it as a short prayer of trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George MacDonald: God's love as a thread too fine to see, and a fire that won't give up. Your line was love will not let go.

Karl Barth wrote theology by the shelf. His great work, the Church Dogmatics, fills thick volume after thick volume, and he never finished it. The story goes that on a lecture visit, a student asked him to sum up his whole life's work in a single sentence. And Barth, the story says, answered with a song from childhood: "Jesus loves me! this I know, for the Bible tells me so." The story is told in more than one version, and people still argue about exactly where and when he said it. But it stuck, maybe because of the surprise in it.

It sounds like a dodge. It isn't. Barth's theology turns on one conviction: we don't climb up to God; God comes down to us. Everything starts with God speaking, God acting, God loving first, in Jesus Christ. That's why he argued so hard with theologians who began from human experience, Schleiermacher among them, whom this path met last week. Now take the song word by word. Jesus: the center is a person, not an idea. Loves: the first thing God says to us is yes. Me: a person, not humanity in general. This I know, for the Bible tells me so: the knowing isn't something worked out alone; it was told, handed over, given. The first letter of John puts it the same way round: "We love him, because he first loved us." And, shorter still: "God is love." Barth's critics found him hard going, and sometimes too sure of himself. His admirers say the thick volumes are, in a way, one long commentary on that children's line. Christians read him both ways. Either way, the scene stays: a man who could talk for volumes, asked for the heart of it all, reached for words a child could sing.

If you're here to learn rather than to pray, notice what each word claims, without needing to agree. Let each word land before the next, then rest in the quiet after.

1270.title: Bonhoeffer's prison questions
1270.hook: in prison he asked who Christ is for us today
1270.howItsDone: Bonhoeffer's prison letters, published after his death, are read in study groups, sermons and retreats; some Christians keep his question in front of them as a way of examining how their faith meets daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barth's simple summary: a whole theology, the story says, in a children's song. Your line was Jesus loves me.

A prison cell in Berlin. Letters go out with the help of guards willing to carry them. The prisoner is Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the Lutheran pastor this path met earlier, held by the Nazi regime and connected to the resistance against it. Outside, the war goes on. Inside, he writes to his friend Eberhard Bethge, and in one of those letters puts down a question he can't stop turning over: who is Christ really, for us today? Not a question for a seminar. A question from a man who didn't know if he'd see the outside again.

Bonhoeffer wasn't asking what Christ meant for people long ago, or what the creeds say in the abstract. He was asking what Christ means for a world where people no longer felt they needed religion to explain things. In his letters he tried out bold phrases, like religionless Christianity, and he warned against using God as a stopgap: a God who only shows up at the edges, where our knowledge runs out or our strength gives way. God, he wrote, should be found at the center of life: in strength as well as weakness, in health and not only in a crisis. In notes for a book he never finished, he called Jesus the man for others, and said the church is only the church when it exists for others. He didn't live to work it out. The Nazi regime executed him before the war ended, and the questions stayed open. Christians still read them differently. Some hear a call to a quieter, more worldly faith, lived out in plain service. Others point out that in another letter he named prayer and doing what is right as the heart of being a Christian in his time, and hear a call to costly discipleship. The question itself is old. Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his own disciples: "But whom say ye that I am?" Bonhoeffer heard it again, in a cell, with the world on fire around him.

segments.voice: Let Bonhoeffer's question sit with you, then bring it closer: who is Christ, for this week, in the life you actually have? If you follow Jesus, notice what answer comes and what answer you wish would come; if you don't, ask what his life seems to mean to the people you know who do. There's no need to land anywhere; just keep the question company.

1271.title: Ultimate concern
1271.hook: Paul Tillich: faith is being grasped by what ultimately matters
1271.howItsDone: Tillich is read in seminaries and by thoughtful seekers; some Christians use his question, what concerns me ultimately, as part of an examination of conscience or a retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's prison questions, asked from a cell in Berlin. Your line was who is Christ today?

What would you give up last? Run down the list slowly: a hobby, a job, a city, money, comfort, your reputation, your plans. Somewhere near the bottom there may be something you'd keep even if all the rest went. The German theologian Paul Tillich, who later taught in America, said that thing tells you something about faith. Not because it's religious; it might not be. Because of where it sits in a life: at the bottom of the list, holding everything else up.

Tillich's phrase is ultimate concern. Faith, he said, is the state of being grasped by what concerns you ultimately. Notice the verb. Not grasping: grasped. You don't pick an ultimate concern the way you pick a topping. It takes hold of you, it asks for everything, and it promises, in some way, to fulfill you. Then he makes an uncomfortable point. Everyone, as Tillich saw it, has something in that place: for one person success, for another a nation, or a person they love. When what sits there isn't truly ultimate, when it's something finite dressed up as everything, he called it idolatry, and said it ends in disappointment. Only God, whom he described as the ground of being, can bear that weight. Some readers connect this with the commandment Jesus called the first: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength." All, and all, and all. And Jesus said it more plainly still: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Tillich has critics. Some say his language about God grows so abstract it loses the God who speaks and acts in the Bible. His defenders say he was trying to reach people for whom the old words had gone quiet. Either way, his question cuts close: whatever you'd give up last, can it hold what you're asking it to hold?
screen: `GRASPED, NOT GRASPING` · `FINITE THINGS DRESSED AS EVERYTHING` · `WITH ALL THY HEART` · `WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you give your best hours to, what you'd sacrifice for, what you're most afraid of losing, and let the honest answer come, even if it surprises you. Hold it gently, without judging it. If you pray, you can offer that answer to God just as it is.

1272.title: The serenity prayer
1272.hook: Reinhold Niebuhr is credited with the prayer asking serenity, courage and wisdom
1272.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the serenity prayer daily or keep it on a wall at home; it is also said aloud together in some recovery groups and other gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul Tillich and ultimate concern: faith as being grasped by what matters most. Your line was what matters most.

It hangs on kitchen walls. It's printed on mugs and bookmarks and tucked into wallets. Some people can say it by heart without remembering where they learned it. It's a short prayer, and its request is plain: serenity to accept the things that can't be changed, courage to change the things that can, and wisdom to know the difference. The prayer is credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, an American preacher and theologian, and it has traveled a long way from any one pulpit since.

Look at the shape of it. The first two requests pull in opposite directions. One says: let it go. The other says: get up and do something. A person can lean too far either way, fighting what will never move, or shrugging at what could be fixed by Thursday. The prayer won't pick a side. It asks for both, and then for the thing that decides between them. That last request is the hinge. The letter of James says: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him." Upbraideth not: in James's picture, God doesn't scold anyone for asking. The Gospels show both halves in a single night. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." He really asks, and he really yields. Paul tells a smaller story about a thorn in the flesh. He begged for it to be taken away, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The letter never says the thorn left. When he is weak, Paul goes on, then he is strong. So the serenity prayer isn't a shrug. Its last line asks for judgment, fresh each time: is this a wall to accept, or a door to push? Some days the honest answer is, not sure yet. Which is exactly why the prayer asks for wisdom.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one situation that's been sitting on your chest, and sort it gently: set down the part you can't change, the past, another person's choices, and hold up the part you can, even a little, a phone call, an apology, a first step. If you pray, you can say the serenity prayer slowly, in the words you know, pausing after each line; if you don't, just let the sorting happen.
The serenity prayer. A short prayer credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, asking for serenity, for courage, and for the wisdom to tell which one this moment needs.
Your line: know the difference. Serenity, courage, and the wisdom between them. See you tomorrow.

1273.title: Attention as prayer
1273.hook: Simone Weil held that attention, taken to its highest, is prayer
1273.howItsDone: Some Christians practice prayer as attention, sitting quietly before God without words, or praying while giving full attention to a task or a person; Simone Weil's essays are read in many settings as a guide to this.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the serenity prayer: serenity, courage, and the wisdom between them. Your line was know the difference.

A student sits over a geometry problem and can't crack it. The hour runs out. The page is a mess of crossed-out lines. Was the hour wasted? Simone Weil, a French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ, said no. In an essay written for students, she argued that real effort of attention is never lost, even when the problem stays unsolved. What's being trained, she said, isn't geometry. It's attention. And attention, taken to its highest, is the same thing as prayer.

Weil means something specific by attention. Not frowning. Not clenching your jaw. She describes it as more like waiting: holding your own thoughts back, empty and ready, so that what's really there can come in. Straining gets in the way. That's why she cared about schoolwork. A Latin translation, a math proof: done with real attention, she thought, each one stretches the same capacity the soul uses to turn toward God. Then she turns it toward people. Love of neighbor, Weil wrote, comes down to being able to ask someone, what are you going through? And then actually to look and listen, without rushing to fix them. She thought that kind of attention was rare, and close to a miracle. Luke has a scene she'd recognize, one this path met earlier. Jesus is a guest in a home. Martha is busy serving. Her sister Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." Martha complains, and Jesus answers: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part." Readers take this in different ways. Some stress that Martha's work is good too, just anxious. Some hear Mary as a picture of prayer itself. Weil's lens adds one thing: Mary isn't doing nothing. She's attending. A phone buzzing face-down on the table. A friend talking while you plan your reply. A prayer said while thinking about lunch. Weil's point lands on all of them: the opposite of prayer may not be doubt. It may be distraction.

Choose one sound in the room, a clock, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing, and listen to it only, without naming or explaining it. When your mind slides off, notice where it went and come back without scolding; attention, for Weil, is a kind of waiting. If you pray, you can let this listening be your prayer, with no words at all.
Attention as prayer. Simone Weil's claim that attention, taken to its highest, is the same as prayer: open, waiting, and fully there, for God and for a neighbor.
Your line: attention is prayer. Even an hour on an unsolved problem trains it. Until tomorrow.

1274.title: Merton's mountain
1274.hook: a young writer becomes a Trappist monk and writes about contemplation and peace
1274.howItsDone: Some Christians set aside time for silent contemplative prayer, alone or in groups, and some go on retreat at monasteries such as Gethsemani; Merton's books are read by Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox Christians alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simone Weil: attention, taken to its highest, is prayer. Your line was attention is prayer.

A young man in New York has tried what a clever young writer can try: parties, politics, poetry, ambition. He becomes a Catholic, and then he goes further. He travels to a monastery in the Kentucky hills called Gethsemani and asks to join the Trappists, monks who live by prayer, work and long stretches of silence. His name is Thomas Merton. Later he tells the story of that road in a memoir called The Seven Storey Mountain. Today closes a week of voices with the monk who climbed into silence, and what he found waiting there.

You might expect a monk's message to be: leave the world behind. Merton wrote about contemplation, which he describes as a kind of waking up: becoming aware of God's life, the reality underneath all the noise. And he kept insisting it isn't a prize reserved for monks. Years into monastic life, he's sent into the city of Louisville on an errand. Standing on a busy corner in the shopping district, surrounded by strangers, he writes that he was suddenly overwhelmed with the realization that he loved all these people, that they were his and he theirs, that they could not be alien to one another even though they were total strangers. He compares it to waking from a dream of separateness. The monk who left the world found it again on a shopping street. Silence wasn't a wall against people. It was where he learned to see them. A psalm puts the invitation in a handful of words: "Be still, and know that I am God." Merton's life reads like a long commentary on its first two words. He went on to write about peace, war and racial justice, the same stillness turned outward. Look back over this week of voices: MacDonald's love that won't let go, Barth's song, Bonhoeffer's question, Tillich's concern, the serenity prayer, Weil's attention. And Merton, finding the crowd at the end of the silence.

No words for this one, no list to work through: let the sounds of the room come and go, and when a thought arrives, let it pass like a car on the street outside, heard and then gone. If you pray, you can rest in the line be still, and know that I am God, then let even that go quiet; if you don't, simply be still.
Merton's mountain. Thomas Merton's climb into a monastery's silence, where he found contemplation, and found the world waiting there too.
Your line: contemplation is for all. Not a prize kept for monks. Same time tomorrow.

chat.says: Thomas Merton became a monk. So he wanted to get away from people, right?
options: Not in the end. Silence taught him to see people; on a busy corner he felt he loved them all.
Yes. He wrote that prayer works best far from cities, so he never thought of people again.
Yes. He said contemplation is a prize only monks can reach, not ordinary people.
chat.meaning: Merton insisted contemplation isn't only for monks, and on a Louisville street corner he woke from a dream of separateness, loving the strangers around him.
